name: MBA placement
summary: MBA placement interviews, for both summer internships and final roles, commonly start from your CV: interviewers pick a line and go deep, ask why you chose an MBA and the function, and test business sense with a guesstimate or a short case. Some companies add a group discussion or a short presentation, and the questions shift with the function, such as marketing, finance, consulting or operations.
rounds: CV shortlisting, sometimes with an online test
Group discussion or group case for some companies
One or more personal interviews on your CV, why an MBA, the function and your past work
A guesstimate, case or functional questions, often within the interviews
Final round with senior leaders or HR, sometimes on the same day
looks_for: A clear, believable story: past work or studies, why an MBA, why this function
Depth on every line of your CV
Structured thinking in guesstimates and cases
Functional basics for the role: marketing, finance, operations or HR
Awareness of the industry and the company
Maturity, leadership and teamwork from college or work

questions.text: Tell me about a time you led a team during your MBA, such as a club, a live project or a competition.
covers: The goal and the team
What you did yourself, including one hard call
The result and what you learned about leading peers

questions.text: Tell me about a disagreement in a group project and how it was resolved.
covers: Both sides of the disagreement, stated fairly
What you did to move things forward
The outcome and how the group worked afterwards

questions.text: What was your biggest achievement before your MBA, and what exactly was your part in it?
covers: Why it was hard and why it mattered
Your own actions, separated from the team's
A measurable result

questions.text: Tell me about a setback, such as a competition you lost, a poor grade or a job that didn't work out.
covers: What happened, owned honestly
What you took from it
How it shaped a later decision

questions.text: Estimate the number of cars sold in Bengaluru in a year.
covers: An approach: households and car ownership, then new buyers plus replacements
Clear, rounded assumptions said out loud
A sense-check, and which assumption matters most

questions.text: Walk me through your summer internship project: the problem, what you did and what changed.
covers: The business problem and why the company cared
Your approach, data and one key insight
Your recommendation and what the company did with it

questions.text: A biscuit brand is losing market share in small towns. How would you work out why?
covers: Splitting by region, channel and pack size, and checking distribution first
Price, competitors and changing tastes
A recommendation and how you'd test it

questions.text: For a marketing role: how would you launch a new shampoo aimed at college students?
covers: The target customer, the positioning and how it differs from what's on the shelf
Price, pack size, channels and promotion
How you'd judge the launch in the first three months

questions.text: For a finance role: which three numbers would you look at first to judge a company's health, and why?
covers: Choices such as revenue growth, operating margin, cash flow and debt levels
Why each one matters and what it can hide
Comparing with past years and with competitors

questions.text: For an operations role: how would you cut delivery times for an online grocery business?
covers: Mapping the order journey from order to doorstep and timing each step
Ideas such as stores closer to customers, faster picking and better routing
The cost of each idea and how you'd test it

questions.text: What's the difference between a brand manager's job and a sales manager's job?
covers: Brand: the product's positioning, pricing, communication and growth over time
Sales: getting the product to customers and channels and hitting targets
How the two work together, with an example

questions.text: Tell me about a business development you've followed recently. What would you have done in that company's place?
covers: The development, summarised in two sentences
Your view of why the company acted as it did
What you'd have done, and the risk in your choice

questions.text: Group discussion: 'Will online shopping replace local shops?' What would you say first, and how would you handle someone who dominates?
covers: A clear opening view with one fact or example
Bringing in quieter people and steering back to the topic politely
A summary that pulls the group's points together

questions.text: Walk me through your CV and why you chose an MBA.
covers: A short, ordered story of your studies and work
The reason for the MBA, linked to what came before
The role you want now and why

questions.text: Why this function, and why our company?
covers: What draws you to the function, shown by your internship or projects
Something specific about the company: its brands, markets or way of working
What you'd bring in your first year

questions.text: Why are you moving from your earlier field, such as engineering or IT, to a business role?
covers: What in your earlier work pulled you towards business
Skills that carry over, such as analysis or working with clients
How you've been filling the gaps

questions.text: Where do you see yourself five years after your MBA?
covers: A realistic path in this function
The skills and responsibility you want to build
How this company fits into that

tips: Know every line of your CV well enough to talk about it for two minutes; interviewers commonly pick lines at random.
Have one clear, honest answer to 'why MBA' that links your past, the course and the role you want.
For guesstimates, state your approach first, round the numbers and sense-check the answer.
Read business news daily in the weeks before placements, focusing on the sectors you're applying to.
Prepare a short version of your summer project that someone from a different function would follow.
In a group discussion, a clear structure and a good summary often count for more than talking the most.
